text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
--- Telecoms group Tele Danmark is to start a new commercial radio channel in March 1997, breaking Danish state radio's nationwide monopoly and aiming to reach 140,000 listeners a day.

--- Upmarket audio/video/television manufacturer Bang & Olufsen (B & O) is being accused of exploiting its dominant position on the Danish domestic market by excluding competitors from stores selling its products.
--- Danish National Statistics Office figures show that Britain seems set to replace Sweden as Denmark's second largest trading partner next year after Germany.

--- The biggest hacker court case ever in Scandinavia against six Danes is now approaching its end at Roskilde Assizes, near Copenhagen. The six hackers are accused of penetrating computer systems at U.S. Pentagon defence headquarters in Washington and can expect severe sentences.

--- Fresh European Union pressure will probably force Denmark to allow beer and soda in cans. Up to now environmental minister Svend Auken has insisted on retaining the present returnable bottle system and banning drinks in tins.
--- More than 70 percent of all Danish companies expect to use the Euro as a means of payment by the year 2000, a new survey shows.

--- The Turkish Embassy in Denmark is refusing to revoke a list of five Danes declared persona non grata in Turkey. The Danes in question, largely politicians, have been blacklisted by Ankara for participating in a Kurdish parliamentary hearing in Copenhagen last March.
